notes.1a: The majority of candidates answered this question correctly. The most common error was to give a time representing the maximum speed.
notes.1b: Most candidates answered this question well. However weaker candidates used an incorrect transformation of speed = distance/time, i.e. distance = speed/time.
notes.1ci: (ii) The majority of candidates identified B as the forces acting on the cyclist at a time of 20 seconds. Most of these candidates then gave a correct explanation for their choice. Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0625 Physics November 2016
notes.2a: A number of candidates found this question challenging. The majority of these failed to subtract the original length from the extended length for each of the loads. A common error was to identify one of the extensions and to add this to the values in the table.
notes.2b: Most candidates gained at least partial credit in this question. However candidates often gave vague or unclear descriptions of how to improve the accuracy of the measurements.
notes.2ci: The majority of candidates labelled the lines correctly and gave an adequate explanation.
notes.2cii: The majority of candidates drew a suitable line for elastic band C.
notes.3a: Only the stronger candidates answered this question fully correctly and recognised that the force must be applied further away from the pivot than the support for the barrier.
notes.3b: Many candidates answered this question well but a large number thought that moment = force ÷ distance from pivot.
notes.3c: Many candidates found this question challenging. In many answers there was confusion of forces and distances in attempts at principle of moments calculations.
notes.4ai: Many candidates answered correctly but a significant number thought that the energy gained by the load due to its increase in height was kinetic energy.
notes.4aii: This was only answered well by the strongest candidates. A common error was to state that the energy contaminated the surroundings.
notes.4aiii: Many candidates correctly stated the principle of conservation of energy but few went on to correctly link the principle to the example of the motor.
notes.4b: The vast majority of candidates answered this question well but there were some vague and imprecise statements about benefits and problems associated with coal-fired power stations.
notes.5ai: The majority of candidates answered this question well.
notes.5aii: The majority of candidates gained partial credit but very few went on to gain full credit by showing total internal reflection of the ray at the flat surface.
notes.5bi: -(iii) The majority of candidates correctly drew the ray from the headlights to the observer, but very few correctly labelled the diagram, and even fewer stated a correct version of the law of reflection.
notes.6a: Only the strongest candidates gained full credit for this question. Many candidates gave descriptions of evaporation here, and others gave only vague and imprecise statements about the arrangement and movement of molecules in the liquid water and the water vapour.
notes.6b: The majority of candidates recognised the process of evaporation, but only more able candidates gave adequate descriptions. A common error was to attempt to describe boiling.
notes.6c: Many candidates answered this question well. Weaker candidates used incorrect transformations of the equation pressure = force/area. Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0625 Physics November 2016
notes.7a: Most candidates correctly identified the missing wave from the spectrum.
notes.7b: The majority of candidates answered correctly.
notes.7c: A number of candidates failed to answer correctly with all three options being chosen in roughly the same proportion.
notes.7d: Only more able candidates were capable of giving a clear difference between sound waves and electromagnetic waves.
notes.8a: A number of candidates failed to put an A or a V in either meter.
notes.8b: The majority of candidates correctly calculated the resistance of the wire. Weaker candidates used an incorrect transformation of V = I R.
notes.8c: Only the strongest candidates were able to link a decrease in current to the increased resistance of the thinner wire.
notes.9a: The majority of candidates answered well. Weaker candidates gave materials such as copper and steel.
notes.9bi: Many candidates correctly calculated the output voltage of the transformer. In weaker answers, numbers were given in some form of ratio, which could not be given any credit.
notes.9bii: Only more able candidates linked the step down transformer to either the number of turns on the coils or the change in voltage from one coil to another.
notes.9c: While there were a number of strong answers, the vast majority of candidates failed to clearly describe the advantages of transmitting electricity at a high voltage.
notes.10a: This question was generally answered well.
notes.10bi: Many candidates correctly identified end A and end B. Weaker candidates often had the poles reversed.
notes.10bii: (iii) While many candidates gained partial credit on this question, there was a lack of precision in a large number of answers.
notes.10c: Some candidates were able to give 2 distinct answers. However the majority only gave one answers but gave it twice with different phrasing.
notes.11a: The most able candidates gave descriptions which were often very clear and precise, supported by good diagrams. The majority of candidates however, showed little familiarity with how to use the equipment to demonstrate electromagnetic induction.
notes.11b: The majority of candidates answered this question correctly.
notes.11c: Many candidates were able to give suitable methods of increasing the e.m.f. in the wire. Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0625 Physics November 2016
notes.12a: Only the most able candidates gained full credit. The most common error was to state that electrons were one of the particles found in the nucleus, whilst others simply gave nucleons as the name of a particle in the nucleus.
notes.12b: Many candidates gave clear explanations of what is meant by the term isotope . The most common error was to state that the number of neutrons was the same, and that the number of protons differed. Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0625 Physics November 2016
